text: The Taddei Tondo, also known as The Virgin and Child with the Infant St. John, is an unfinished marble relief tondo created by the Italian Renaissance artist Michelangelo Buonarroti. It is the only marble sculpture by Michelangelo in Great Britain and is part of the permanent collection of the Royal Academy of Arts in London. Dating to Michelangelo's time in Florence before his move to Rome in 1505, the tondo was commissioned by Taddeo Taddei, a patron and friend of Raphael. According to art historian Vasari, while working on his David, Michelangelo blocked out but did not finish two marble tondi—one for Taddeo Taddei, now in his house, and another for Bartolomeo Pitti, which was begun but left unfinished. The tondo features a seated Virgin Mary with the baby Jesus dynamically sprawled across her lap, turning and looking back over his right shoulder toward the infant Saint John the Baptist, who stands before him, looking down and holding a fluttering bird. The bird is most likely a goldfinch, symbolizing the Passion, and the unfinished portion below it may have been intended as a crown of thorns. John, patron saint of Florence, with his attribute of a baptismal bowl, crosses his arms, possibly alluding to the cross. The work is executed using only a point and claw chisel, driven hard and with great energy, creating a sense of surface unity without drill marks. The Christ child is the only figure highly finished (except for the feet), St. John is less finished, Mary is the least finished, and the background is only roughly executed. These variations in texture are believed to establish the relative status of the figures and enhance compositional depth. On the reverse of the relief, a ligature combining the letters L and A is present, likely the mark of Lapo d'Antonio di Lapo, a carver and assistant active at the Opera del Duomo from 1506–1507; a chisel blow from this phase caused a hairline crack in the Virgin’s face, possibly due to Michelangelo’s decision to continue working despite the damage, possibly due to material constraints or confidence in his ability to work around flaws. The missing segment at the bottom right may result from an excess of Michelangelo’s "direct attack." Work on the tondo ceased at some point; five holes in the outer rim were intended for fixings and are variously dated. The tondo was originally in the Palazzo Taddei and documented there in 1568, but by 1678, the family had moved to a new residence near San Remigio. It was later taken to Rome, where it was acquired by Sir George Beaumont in 1822 from Jean-Baptiste Wicar. Initially displayed at Beaumont’s house in Grosvenor Square, it was bequeathed to the Royal Academy in 1830 and installed at Somerset House, then moved with the Academy to the east wing of the new National Gallery building in 1836, remaining there until the Academy relocated to Burlington House in 1868. Except for an exhibition at the Victoria and Albert Museum in 1960, it has been housed in various Academy locations since. In 1989, the discovery of a hairline crack led to the decision to provide a permanent home for the tondo. It was cleaned with dichloromethane swabs and clay poultices to remove residues of nineteenth-century plaster casts, oil-based release agents, packing materials, beeswax, pine resin adhesives, and other surface accretions. The tondo was left unwaxed and without any coating, as it is not finished and was originally unpolished, like Michelangelo’s David when completed. Since the opening of the Sackler Wing of Galleries in 1991, it has been on free public display on the top floor, behind protective glass for preventive conservation against air pollution and vandalism. The tondo format was a hallmark of the Florentine Renaissance, with leading artists such as Filippo Lippi, Botticelli, Luca Signorelli, Piero di Cosimo, Fra Bartolomeo, Andrea del Sarto, Leonardo da Vinci (in a lost work), and Raphael creating tondi. Michelangelo experimented with the form, producing the Doni tondo (his only panel painting documented in contemporary sources) and beginning two unfinished tondo sculptures—the Pitti and Taddei tondi—after which he never returned to the tondo form in either medium. Raphael studied and reworked the tondo in two drawings: the versi of The Storming of Perugia at the Louvre and compositional studies for the Madonna del Prato at Chatsworth House, and also applied Michelangelo’s twisting Christ child pose in the Bridgewater Madonna. Shortly after arriving in England, the tondo was sketched by Wilkie, who wrote to Beaumont that it was "the chief talk of all our artists" and a "great addition to our stock of art," justifying Michelangelo’s great reputation. Cockerell noted in his diary that the subject "seems growing from the marble & emerging into life," as if being formed from an unformed mass. Constable, upon its arrival at the Royal Academy, published a letter in the Athenaeum of 3 July 1830 praising its lighting, which highlighted the more finished parts and made the less perfect areas appear as masses of shadow, creating the effect of a rich picture in chiaroscuro. The tondo is an outstanding technical study piece, with plaster casts found at the Victoria and Albert Museum and Fitzwilliam Museum. Many of Michelangelo’s works are unfinished, and while some are viewed as completed, the nineteenth-century critic Eugène Guillaume described his "non finito" as an expressive device for infinite suggestiveness.
